message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to two different orders—Carnivora and Perissodactyla, respectively.  
Their most recent common ancestor is the last common ancestor of all **Laurasiatherian** mammals, the clade that includes carnivores, ungulates, bats, cetaceans, and a few other groups.  

This ancestor lived roughly **90–100 million years ago**, during the late Cretaceous/early Paleogene. It was a small, generalized mammal that gave rise to the divergent lineages that eventually produced modern lions, zebras, and many other Laurasiatherian species.

The lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) are both mammals, but belong to different orders: lions are Carnivora, zebras are Perissodactyla. Their common ancestor would be at the level of the last common ancestor of all placental mammals? Actually, the last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals? Wait, let's think: Carnivora and Perissodactyla diverged from each other within Laurasiatheria. The last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla would be the last common ancestor of all Laurasiatheria. That is older than the last common ancestor of all placental mammals. So the common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of all Laurasiatheria, which lived about 90 million years ago. Or "They share a common ancestor that is a mammal that lived around 70 million years ago." The last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla is about 90 million years ago. So the answer: "The last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of all Laurasiatheria, which lived about 90 million years ago."
